summary: Extends IS-IS Traffic Engineering (RFC 5305) to distribute network-performance information, such as latency, in a scalable way. This matters in networks like financial data networks where such measures matter as much as other metrics for path selection. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Sometimes the fastest road matters more than the shortest. This lets routers share how quick each link is, such as how long messages take, so they can pick well.

questions: what is is-is te metric extensions
what is the anomalous bit in is-is
subtitle: How IS-IS routers share link delay, loss and bandwidth so paths can be chosen on performance, not just cost.

tldr.problem: In some networks, such as financial data networks, latency matters as much as any other metric for choosing a path, but IS-IS Traffic Engineering had no way to distribute performance data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8570 defines seven new sub-TLVs (types 33 to 39) carrying link delay, min/max delay, delay variation, loss, and residual, available and utilized bandwidth, plus rules for thresholds, throttling and an Anomalous bit.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7810 and fixes an ambiguity in the length of the bandwidth sub-TLVs. It only distributes the data; measuring it and acting on it are out of scope.

today: RFC 8570 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2019. It obsoletes RFC 7810, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Performance Data Matters
sections.content:
In some networks, such as financial information networks, the ability to get market data in "real time" and to trade faster than the competition is worth a great deal. Hop count or cost then becomes only tangentially important as a routing metric. Path selection is better made on performance data such as latency.

RFC 8570 extends the Extended IS Reachability TLV from RFC 5305 to distribute such data: link delay, delay variation, packet loss, residual bandwidth and available bandwidth. Receivers can use it inside the routing protocol (for example by replacing cost with latency), to enhance Constrained Shortest Path First (CSPF), or to feed an ALTO server. For CSPF it can help set up, fail over and fail back paths made with RSVP-TE.

The scope is narrow. The document only covers dissemination. How the numbers are measured, or what to do with them, is left out. It does say that delay measurement SHOULD NOT vary much with offered load, so queuing delays SHOULD NOT be included.
sections.eli5: Imagine choosing a route to school. Sometimes you care about the quickest way, not the shortest. This document gives routers a way to share how quick each road is. It does not say how to time the roads.

sections.title: The New Sub-TLVs and the A Bit
sections.content:
The extensions are new sub-TLVs registered in the "Sub-TLVs for TLVs 22, 23, 141, 222, and 223" registry. They nest inside the Extended IS Reachability TLV (type 22), the Inter-AS Reachability TLV (type 141) and the MT-ISN TLV (type 222). Seven types are defined, 33 to 39.

Three of them (types 33, 34 and 36) carry an Anomalous (A) bit. When it is clear, the sub-TLV describes steady-state performance, which could be used to build a performance topology or check backup paths. When link performance violates a configured threshold, the sub-TLV is advertised with the A bit set. A receiving node, such as an LSP ingress, can then decide whether to fail traffic over to a backup path or compute a new one. When performance improves past a configured reuse threshold, the sub-TLV can be re-advertised with the A bit cleared, allowing failback.

Sub-TLVs without an A bit cannot be used for failover. The bit was left out of some of them on purpose, to help avoid oscillations.

Encoding rules: bandwidth MUST be IEEE floating-point in bytes per second, delay and delay variation MUST be integers in microseconds, and loss MUST be a percentage of packets sent. All values except residual bandwidth MUST be rolling averages over a configurable period.
sections.eli5: Each link carries a little report card. If a link starts doing badly, it raises a warning flag. When it gets better, the flag comes down, and routers can move traffic back.

sections.title: The Seven Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Each sub-TLV reports a value for the direction from the advertising router to its neighbor, so the numbers are one-way ("unidirectional").

  • Link Delay (33): average delay in microseconds, in a 24-bit field. The maximum value, 16,777,215, means the delay is at least that much and may be larger.
  • Min/Max Link Delay (34): minimum and maximum measured delay, each 24 bits. They may be equal.
  • Delay Variation (35): average variation in microseconds, 24 bits. A value of 0 means it has not been measured.
  • Link Loss (36): 24-bit loss percentage with a basic unit of 0.000003%. The value (2^24 - 2) stands for 50.331642%, the highest expressible loss, and larger measurements SHOULD be encoded as that maximum.
  • Residual Bandwidth (37): the maximum bandwidth minus bandwidth allocated to RSVP-TE label switched paths, aggregated across priorities. For a bundled link it is the sum of component residuals.
  • Available Bandwidth (38): residual bandwidth minus the measured bandwidth used by traffic that is not on RSVP-TE paths.
  • Utilized Bandwidth (39): the actual measured utilization of the link.

Residual bandwidth differs from the unreserved bandwidth of RFC 5305, which is taken from the maximum reservable bandwidth and given per priority. The two can be used together, for example residual for weighted ECMP and unreserved for call admission control.

Reserved fields MUST be set to 0 on send and ignored on receipt. Sub-TLVs 33, 34 and 36 carry the A bit; the others do not. IS-IS TE Metric Extensions may be used without a TE subsystem, but Interface Address and Neighbor Address sub-TLVs MUST still be present.
sections.eli5: There are seven kinds of note a link can send: how long messages take, the fastest and slowest, how bumpy it is, how many get lost, and three about how much room is left or in use.

sections.title: Thresholds, Suppression and Stability
sections.content:
Values in all sub-TLVs except min/max delay and residual bandwidth MUST be an average, or come from a filter reasonably representative of one. Min and max delay come from the lowest and highest measured value over an interval, or from a filter that compensates for outliers. The measurement interval, filter coefficients and advertisement intervals MUST be configurable per sub-TLV.

Implementations SHOULD offer configurable accelerated advertisement thresholds. If a measurement crosses a configured bound, or differs from the last advertised value by more than a threshold, the advertisement is sent immediately. Sub-TLVs with an A bit SHOULD also have a threshold that decides when performance is anomalous, and the A bit is cleared after performance stays back inside it for one or more advertisement intervals. To prevent oscillation, only the high threshold or the low threshold, not both, may trigger a given sub-TLV.

When values change only a little, implementations SHOULD suppress re-advertisement or lengthen the refresh period. Only the accelerated thresholds may shorten it.

For stability in large networks, the default measurement interval SHOULD be 30 seconds. Announcements MUST be throttleable with configurable timers, the minimum periodicity is one announcement per second, and the default SHOULD be 120 seconds. The inter-update timer SHOULD NOT be lower than the measurement interval. Each sub-TLV MUST be individually enableable and disableable, and implementations SHOULD allow static or manual override of dynamic measurements. Unrecognized sub-TLVs are silently ignored, as in RFC 5305.
sections.eli5: Routers should not shout every time a number wiggles a tiny bit. They only speak up for big changes, and otherwise report at a calm, steady pace.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The advertised delay and bandwidth values could be sensitive, and an operator may not want to disclose them. The RFC also points to its stability guidance, and says implementations SHOULD follow it to reduce the risk of instability.

It expects IS-IS to be used mostly within one operator's infrastructure. Still, if the sub-TLVs travel over insecure links, a man-in-the-middle attacker could delay real-time data to a given site or destination. The Link State PDU cryptographic authentication of RFC 5304 mitigates this risk.
sections.eli5: Link reports can reveal private details about a network, and a sneaky listener could mess with them. Locking the messages with a secret check protects them.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7810
sections.content:
RFC 8570 obsoletes RFC 7810. Errata ID 5293 showed that in RFC 7810 the length given for sub-TLVs 37, 38 and 39 was 4, which did not include the RESERVED field shown in their figures. Some implementations used length 4 and left out the field, while others kept it and used length 5. These choices are not interoperable, so a bis version was produced.

The fix omits the unused RESERVED field and uses length 4, matching the equivalent OSPF TE specification (RFC 7471) and the BGP-LS specification (RFC 8571). Errata ID 5486 is also corrected: the definition of available bandwidth for bundled links was circular, and now sums the component link residual bandwidths. Some minor editorial corrections were also made.
sections.eli5: Two groups built the same thing slightly differently, so their gadgets did not fit together. This update picks one way so everyone matches.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Anomalous bit: set when the measured delay exceeds its configured maximum threshold.

fields.name: RESERVED
fields.desc: Set to 0 on send, ignored on receipt.
